title: Benefits application portal
brief: People apply for food, health or housing help on a state site. Forms are long, people save drafts and upload documents, and a caseworker team reviews each one. The last week of the month is busy, and an auditor checks the privacy and access controls once a year.

clarify.a: No. Someone may be applying for help to eat. A saved form must stay saved.

clarify.q: How fast must an email "we got your application" go out?
clarify.a: Within minutes. It can wait in a line when the site is busy.
The closing days of a month can bring four times the usual traffic over several hours.

clarify.q: Who looks at the forms afterwards?
clarify.a: Caseworkers, through an admin tool that runs heavy reports.

notes: Public agencies often have small budgets; cost counts.
A "write" is saving a draft or submitting an application.

Scored data retention: at least 2555 days on active authoritative stores. Copies used only for search or reports can be rebuilt. Local device history and rollup policies still require the separate protocol check.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

numbers.label: Page views and saves at peak

hints: Which work can wait a few minutes without anyone minding?
Confirmation emails and big reports can use a queue and workers. Uploaded documents belong in object storage, not the database.
The audit wants a signed-in identity, an audit log, key-managed encryption, backups and a retention rule. Connect servers to each.

editorial.summary: This is a patient, correct system. The surge is slow and moderate, so a small autoscaled fleet and a cache are enough. The point is to build proof in from day one: identity, audit, encryption, backups, retention.

designs.name: Small, safe, audit-ready
designs.why: A load balancer fronts three servers in two zones. Applications live in a two-zone SQL database; documents go to object storage; confirmation emails are queued. Identity, a key service, an audit log and backups give the auditor what they need.

tradeoffs: Pointing the caseworker reports at a replica keeps the heavy queries away from people saving forms, at the price of a second database.
Synchronous copies make saves a few milliseconds slower and mean a zone failure cannot lose an application.
Object storage for documents is a fraction of the cost of database storage and is retained cheaply for years.
A modest 99.5 percent target is about 3.6 hours of downtime a month; going higher would need a second region and costs far more than this budget allows.
editorial.realWorld: State benefits systems are often judged on how they behave in the last days of a month or a sign-up period, not on average load (approx.). Many run on a few servers and one database and rely on queues for notices and on cloud storage for scanned documents.

correctness.prompt: Benefits application portal: The same request is delivered twice, and a worker can crash after saving it. What uniqueness constraint and transaction would keep one durable result?
correctness.discussion: Choose a stable business operation id and enforce a unique constraint in the authoritative store. Insert the id, apply the change and save its result in one transaction. A retry returns that result. Recording the id before the change can lose work after a crash; recording it afterwards can apply the change twice. If work continues through a queue, commit an outbox entry in the same transaction and deduplicate at each consumer.

fields.label: The server commits a change, then crashes before replying. The client retries. What happens?
options: Commit the operation id, effect and result atomically; return that result on retry
Record the id first, then apply the change in a separate write
fields.explanation: Recording the id separately can either lose an operation or apply it twice. The effect and deduplication result must commit together.

fields.label: The server acknowledges a write just before its storage fails. Which evidence meets the stated recovery point?
options: A queued backup request with no completed durable copy
A durable copy across the required failure boundary before acknowledgement
fields.explanation: A scheduled copy is not a completed copy. Match acknowledgement and recovery to the stated loss boundary.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 75 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $4515. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
